official_first: Follow active emergency alerts, official broadcasts, and on-site instructions first.
household_summary: 4-person · 3-day example: 24 L drinking water, ~46 L total safe water (23 × 2 L bottles, incl. drinking), 36 servings of instant meals & canned goods; adjust to your household.

communication_loss.first_action: If evacuation is needed, evacuate first. Check local announcements or a battery-powered radio for updates.
communication_loss.paper_note: Do not assume an alert is over simply because you cannot hear announcements.

paper_checkpoints.condition: Do not return or depart just because time has passed. Follow new alerts and on-site instructions first.

rows.text: Account for companions, check nearby hazards, and listen to broadcasts. Do not drive to schools during air raids.
Check drinking water, essential meds, and care items. Report your status when safe and communications allow.
Check remaining supplies and distribution points. Before long-distance travel, verify official orders, routes, and support.

playbook.label: First 24h
playbook.title: First 24 Hours After an Alert
playbook.intro: Checkpoints are measured from when the alert was first confirmed. Timing for shelter, return, or travel depends on on-site hazards and official orders.

rows.title: Take protective action for the alert
rows.text: Follow the first action for your alert. If caring for children or anyone needing assistance, guide them to shelter first. If your go-bag is out of reach, do not delay evacuation to look for it.

rows.title: Account for people and nearby hazards
rows.text: Check everyone with you and look for smoke or flooding. Do not leave shelter just because noise stops; listen to on-site announcements or a battery radio.

rows.title: Separated family members shelter in place
rows.text: At work, school, or home, follow local site instructions. Caregivers should not drive to schools during an air raid. Share your location once safe and connected.

rows.title: Use your offline meetup plan if needed
rows.text: Only travel to your written meetup point when movement is officially permitted. Do not set out blindly if someone is overdue; log last known times and places.

rows.title: Prepare for extended stay
rows.text: Check drinking water, prescription medications, care supplies, flashlights, and radio. If power or water remains out, switch to the Outage tab.

playbook.label: Outages & Supply
playbook.title: During Extended Power & Water Outages
playbook.intro: Verify official notices and local safety before sheltering in place. If a new air raid, CBRN, or nuclear alert sounds, switch to that alert's first action immediately.

rows.title: When both power and water are cut
rows.text: Use flashlights and keep fridge/freezer doors shut. Use stored drinking water first. Use DC/USB ports on power banks to avoid AC inverter standby loss. Never run fuel generators or charcoal indoors.

rows.title: Log outage time and prioritize perishables
rows.text: A closed fridge stays cold ~4 hours; a full freezer ~48 hours (~24h half-full). Eat safe perishables first and discard refrigerated food held above 4°C for over 4 hours—never taste to test.

rows.title: Track water, sanitation, and power daily
rows.text: Separate drinking water from washing water. If sewage lines are damaged or restricted, do not flush—use a bag-lined container. Reserve battery power for lighting and radio broadcasts.

rows.title: Check aid before supplies run out
rows.text: Monitor remaining water, food, and medications and locate official supply points. If fire or flooding makes your building unsafe, evacuate immediately.

rows.title: Long-term support and care continuity
rows.text: Reconfirm official water, medical, and care stations. Keep infant feeding and medication routines consistent and update paper contact logs.

playbook.label: Travel Decision
playbook.title: When to Stay vs. When to Relocate
playbook.intro: Plan relocation across pre-crisis, early, and extended phases. Never assume roads become safe simply after a set number of days.

rows.title: Keep documents and transit options ready
rows.text: Prepare family IDs, passports, and contact plans. Check official advisories, operating carriers, entry rules, and destination lodging before planning long-distance travel.

rows.title: Nearest protective shelter comes first
rows.text: Move to the nearest shelter for the alert. Postpone long drives or cross-city meetups until the immediate threat passes.

rows.title: Verify four departure conditions
rows.text: Confirm: (1) official order or local hazard, (2) open route and transport, (3) accessible destination, and (4) support for dependents. Never bypass roadblocks.

rows.title: Compare foot, vehicle, and transit
rows.text: Verify walking distance/ability, official road access and fuel for cars, and confirmed operation for rail/air/ferry before departing.

rows.title: Confirm headcount and local support
rows.text: Record arrival time, check everyone in, share status if possible, and locate water, food, and medical support.

playbook.label: Scenario Matrix
playbook.title: Scenario Transition Matrix
playbook.intro: Multiple events can overlap. Whenever a new alert or evacuation order arrives, follow that scenario's first action immediately.

rows.title: Verify shelters, meetup plans, and core supplies.
rows.text: Monitor official advisories and transit status; review the four departure conditions before considering travel.

rows.title: Use flashlights and stored drinking water.
rows.text: Secure fridge food on Day 1, then audit safe water and supply points daily.

rows.title: Move to the nearest shelter.
rows.text: Confirm headcount and local hazards inside. Do not leave based on silence or elapsed time alone.

rows.title: Check official instructions for shelter type.
rows.text: Different agents require different shelter locations (basement vs. sealed upper floor).

rows.title: Follow official destination and route orders.
rows.text: Verify transit, fuel, and dependent care; report status upon arrival.

rows.title: Track remaining days of water, meds, and care.
rows.text: Update aid locations and reassess immediately if building safety is compromised.

playbook.label: Drills & Audits
playbook.title: Calculating Readiness in Drills
playbook.intro: Check readiness using real numbers from your home. Examples below are illustrative; actual needs vary by household and event.

rows.title: Stored volume ÷ daily household use
rows.text: Example: 12 L safe water ÷ 6 L/day = 2 days. Count cooking/hygiene water separately, and mark unverified water as unknown.

rows.title: Watts (W) × hours (h) = Watt-hours (Wh)
rows.text: Example: 2W light × 4h + 3W radio × 2h + 10W charger × 1h = 24 Wh/day. A 120 Wh usable bank lasts ~5 days before conversion losses.

rows.title: Practice solo and shared caregiving
rows.text: Simulate zero phone/internet: practice evacuating alone with dependents, sheltering separately, and reuniting safely.

rows.title: Verified items ÷ total checked items
rows.text: Example: 3 of 4 core checks verified = 75% audit completion. Note missing items and set the next review date.

rows.title: Combine air raid + comms blackout
rows.text: Using paper only, locate first actions, broadcast channels, and meetup points. Then test outage and supply scenarios.

playbook.label: Equipment Check
playbook.title: Testing Equipment in Peacetime
playbook.intro: Read manuals and test gear before an emergency. Never count equipment as ready unless its limits and condition are verified.

rows.title: Power Banks & Stations
rows.text: Keep the 220V AC inverter OFF to avoid 10–15W idle standby loss and use DC/USB ports only. Prioritize charging in order of radio, flashlight, and phone, follow charger/output limits on a firm, ventilated surface, and stop use immediately if swollen, leaking, smelling odd, or overheating. Log only verified charge levels.

rows.title: Solar Panel to Power Station
rows.text: Verify voltage, current, and connector compatibility in both manuals before connecting. Test discreet indoor window or balcony-interior placement and inspect cables in peacetime to minimize outside visibility during crises; note that window glass and weather cut output sharply, so never rely on rated wattage alone.

rows.title: Portable Water Filters
rows.text: Use stored potable water first. Pair a hollow-fiber filter (for sediment and bacteria) with Aquatabs purification tablets, unscented bleach disinfection, or boiling since most portable filters do not remove viruses. Never drink seawater or chemically/radiologically suspect water—find an alternate source.

rows.title: Portable Stoves & Butane
rows.text: Check manufacture/expiry dates and inspect cans for rust or dents. Keep away from heat, never use indoors without ventilation, avoid oversized pans or double stacking, and detach cans after use.

rows.title: Emergency Fuel Siphoning (Safety First)
rows.text: Only in lawful, extreme emergencies and from your own or an authorized vehicle, extract fuel into a metal jerrycan using a manual hand-siphon pump or gravity hose. NEVER siphon fuel by mouth due to lethal toxic vapor and lung aspiration hazards. Shut off the engine and ignition completely, touch bare vehicle metal to discharge static electricity before opening the cap, and work outdoors far from sparks or flames.

rows.title: Pre-Mapping Nearby Hubs
rows.text: In peacetime, record primary and backup pharmacies, deeper subway stations and underground tunnel links, marts, convenience stores, and civil defense shelter entrances with walking routes on paper maps. Map pins never guarantee open status or access during alerts—evacuation always takes priority over shopping.

playbook.label: Field Skills
playbook.title: Navigation & Hygiene Skills to Practice
playbook.intro: On-site hazards and official orders always take priority. These notes cover general peacetime skills and do not guarantee route safety.

rows.title: Paper Maps & Compass
rows.text: Print maps to shelters and meetup points in peacetime and practice reading scale, landmarks, and bearings. If lost, stop and orient before moving.

rows.title: Natural Direction Finding (Sun, Stars, Trees)
rows.text: Mark the tip of a stick's shadow and mark it again 15 minutes later—the line runs West (first mark) to East (second); or point an analog watch's hour hand at the sun so the bisector to 12 o'clock points South (Northern Hemisphere). At night, extend the line of the Big Dipper's two end bowl stars (Dubhe & Merak) about 5×—or extend perpendicular from the center of Cassiopeia's W about 5×—to find Polaris (true North). Wider tree rings on the south side and moss on the north are rough cues with many exceptions from terrain, wind, and moisture, so always cross-check with sun, stars, or a compass.

rows.title: Trail Marking & Backtracking
rows.text: At junctions and regular intervals, leave clear eye-level markers aligned with your travel direction using stacked stones (cairns), stick arrows, or reflective tape/cloth strips. Look back frequently to memorize reverse landmarks so you can safely backtrack to your origin.

rows.title: Emergency Procedures Over Seat Choice
rows.text: On planes, read safety cards, fasten belts, and note nearest exits. On trains, locate emergency intercoms and lighting and follow crew instructions.

rows.title: Life Jackets & Crew Orders
rows.text: Confirm life jacket fit and location before boarding, and follow crew instructions during incidents.

rows.title: Sanitation: Toilet Shutoff & Bag Sealing
rows.text: Do not assume toilets are unusable on water outage alone, but if sewage is damaged or restricted, follow this sequence: (1) shut off the main water valve and the toilet's supply angle valve; (2) flush once to empty remaining tank water and prevent accidental flushing or backflow; (3) lift the seat, double-seal the bowl with a large plastic sheet or heavy wrap, lower the seat, and double-line with black trash bags using solidifier, cat litter, or baking soda. Place a water-filled plastic bag (water lock) over floor drains to block odors/backflow, wash hands, and store sealed waste separately.

rows.title: Wet Clothing & Hypothermia
rows.text: Move out of wind, remove wet clothes, and layer dry clothes/blankets. Shivering, confusion, or slurred speech signal hypothermia—seek medical help and avoid alcohol or direct open-flame heat.

playbook.label: Wild Survival
playbook.title: Wild Water & Food
playbook.intro: Stored water, rations, and certified life-saving gear always come first. Use these field techniques only as last-resort backups when normal supplies are completely cut off.

rows.title: Collecting Water with Plastic Sheets
rows.text: For a transpiration bag, seal a clear plastic bag tightly around a sunlit, non-toxic broadleaf branch with a small pebble in the lower corner to pool condensation. For a solar still, dig a sunlit pit with a cup in the center, surround it with damp foliage, seal a plastic sheet over the pit with dirt, and place a small stone in the center so condensation drips into the cup. Treat these as supplemental backups—prioritize stored water and official supply points, and never drink seawater.

rows.title: Wild Edible Plants & Roots (Caution)
rows.text: Relatively identifiable wild edibles in Korea include mugwort (ssuk), dandelion, kudzu root, acorns (must be leached repeatedly in water to remove tannins), and pine-needle tea. Strong safety warning: lethal look-alikes such as lily-of-the-valley (confused with wild garlic), water hemlock, jack-in-the-pulpit, and toxic mushrooms are common—NEVER eat any plant or mushroom unless 100% certain, and avoid milky sap, bitter/almond odors, or red berries.

rows.title: Water Survival: Survival Float & Improvised Flotation
rows.text: With the survival float (drownproofing / shrimp float), relax face-down curled loosely in the water using natural buoyancy, and only stroke gently to lift your head for a quick breath before relaxing again to conserve energy. In cold water with a life jacket, hold the HELP posture (knees tucked to chest) to slow hypothermia. Without a life jacket, knot long trouser cuffs, whip them overhead to trap air, and press the waist underwater as an improvised float, or seal empty plastic bottles inside clothing/packs or inflate a dry bag.

rows.title: Improvised Emergency Fishing
rows.text: Cut the top off a plastic bottle and invert it inside as a funnel fish trap baited with insects or rice in shallow water, or stack stones in a V- or U-shaped weir to funnel fish with the current. With line and hook, target slow pools at dawn or dusk. Always cook freshwater fish thoroughly to eliminate parasites.

playbook.label: Transport Safety
playbook.title: Transport Seat Safety
playbook.intro: Seat survival statistics are probabilities that vary by crash scenario. Fastening your seatbelt, locating the nearest exits, and following crew orders always come first.

rows.title: Rear Cabin & Within 5 Rows of Exits
rows.text: Crash statistics show higher survival rates in the rear cabin (~32% fatality vs. ~38% in front), while wing sections sit near fuel tanks. Above all, count rows to the nearest exits (ideally within 5 rows), keep shoes on and seatbacks upright during takeoff and landing, and keep your seatbelt fastened.

rows.title: Middle Rows (Aisle) & Seatbelt
rows.text: On a 45-seat bus, middle-row aisle seats (rows 4–7) offer better buffering against front, rear, and side impacts compared to the very front, very back, or window seats. Wearing a seatbelt cuts fatality risk to roughly one-third—always buckle up and locate emergency exit hammers upon boarding.

rows.title: Center Cars, Rear-Facing Seats & Rules
rows.text: Center cars in a train consist gain buffer protection during collisions or derailments (front cars face direct impact; rear cars face whiplash). Rear-facing seats better support the neck and spine during sudden braking, and dining cars are best avoided. Never step onto tracks during an emergency stop without crew clearance.

rows.title: End Cars, Door Release & Stay Low
rows.text: End cars (first and last) are typically less crowded and closer to platform exits during fire or smoke events. Before departure, note the manual door-release lever (emergency cock) under/beside seats, emergency intercom, and screen-door numbers; in a fire, cover nose and mouth and move low.

rows.title: Rear Center Seat & Ferry Life Jackets
rows.text: In passenger cars, the rear center seat is farthest from front and side impact zones, and seatbelts are essential in every seat. On ferries, check life jacket locations, proper fit, and deck evacuation routes right after boarding, and follow crew announcements.

scenarios.title: Air Raid Alert
scenarios.first_action: Evacuate immediately to the nearest civil defense shelter or safe underground facility.
details: Use emergency stairs in high-rise buildings.
If driving, pull over safely to an open lot or the right shoulder and evacuate.
Avoid basements prone to flooding during heavy rain; if underground shelter is unavailable, move to an interior windowless room in a concrete building.
Keep listening to official government broadcasts inside the shelter.
scenarios.paper_note: Use stairs in high-rises. If underground shelter is flooded or unavailable, shelter in a windowless interior concrete room.

scenarios.title: Civil Defense Warning
scenarios.first_action: Monitor official broadcasts and evacuate immediately if ordered.
details: If permitted by local guidance, help children and people needing mobility assistance evacuate early.
If no evacuation order is active, prepare to move at a moment's notice and keep monitoring updates.
scenarios.paper_note: Prepare to evacuate if no order is active yet; assist children and mobility-impaired family members.

scenarios.title: CBRN Alert
scenarios.first_action: Follow official instructions for shelter location and protective actions.
details: For chemical attacks with shelter-in-place orders, move to an upper-floor room that can be sealed from outside air.
For biological alerts, follow authorities' orders on designated shelter or staying home.
Keep monitoring official broadcasts throughout.
scenarios.paper_note: For chemical indoor-shelter orders, move to a higher-floor room sealed from outside air.

scenarios.title: Nuclear Alert
scenarios.first_action: If there is time before detonation, move quickly to a sealed underground shelter.
details: If caught in the open right after a flash, drop flat and protect your body until the blast wave and debris stop.
Afterward, move to a deep basement or interior concrete structure to reduce fallout exposure and listen to broadcasts.
If fire or structural hazards force you to leave, follow on-site emergency instructions.
scenarios.paper_note: After a flash, drop and cover until blast/debris pass, then shelter deep underground or inside concrete from fallout.

scenarios.title: Power Outage
scenarios.first_action: Use flashlights and keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed.
details: If trapped in an elevator, use the emergency bell or intercom; never force the doors open.
Never run fuel generators or charcoal stoves indoors, in garages, or near windows, doors, or vents.
scenarios.paper_note: Never use fuel generators or charcoal indoors.

scenarios.title: Water Outage
details: Check municipal or utility notices for emergency water truck locations and hours.
Drink water from emergency stations only after confirming it is potable.
Even after tap water returns, follow any boil-water or non-potable advisories.
scenarios.paper_note: Verify operating status and potability before drinking emergency water.

scenarios.title: Peacetime Prep
scenarios.first_action: Verify two civil defense shelters and write them on your family paper sheet.
details: Choose a family meetup point in case communications fail. During an active alert, sheltering comes before reuniting.
Visit shelter entrances in person and verify that your battery-powered radio works and receives stations.
Check SafeKorea maps and local maps in peacetime for primary and backup shelters, pharmacies, stations, and stores. Map pins do not guarantee access during a crisis—never delay evacuation to shop.
Audit your drinking water, shelf-stable foods, and hygiene supplies first, and rotate items nearing expiration.
The 4-person · 3-day example is a starting baseline. SafeKorea recommends 30 days of food/water and 15+ butane canisters—set household targets safely according to your stove and storage.
Check flashlights, batteries, go-bags, and any dependent-care items.
scenarios.paper_note: Set a no-phone meetup spot and test your battery radio reception.
